prompt: You're pairing on Code Review and a teammate says "it works on my machine" about a failing test in CI. What's the most useful next step?

options.text: Mark the test as skipped so the build passes
Compare the CI environment's dependency versions against local
Delete the test file
Re-run CI hoping it passes this time

explanation: Environment drift (dependency versions, OS, timezone) is the single most common cause of local-vs-CI mismatches — check that before touching the test itself.

prompt: During a Code Review session, you notice a function has grown to 300 lines and touches five unrelated concerns. What's the most constructive comment to leave?

options.text: Suggest splitting it into smaller, single-purpose functions with a brief rationale
Ask them to add more comments explaining each section
Request they rewrite it in a different language
Approve it since it technically works

explanation: Long, multi-concern functions are a maintainability risk regardless of whether they currently work — the constructive fix is decomposition, not more comments padding over the structure problem.

prompt: Your team is deciding on Code Review standards. One engineer wants to block all merges without 100% test coverage. What's the more balanced position?

options.text: Agree to 100% coverage everywhere immediately
Remove coverage requirements entirely
Only require coverage on Fridays before releases
Require coverage on new/changed code and critical paths, not a blanket 100%

explanation: Blanket 100% coverage mandates often produce brittle tests written just to hit the number; targeting new code and critical paths gets the real safety benefit without that perverse incentive.

prompt: You're reviewing a design doc where Code Review decisions are made without listing any trade-offs or alternatives considered. What should you ask for?

options.text: The alternatives that were considered and why they were rejected
Nothing — the doc author is senior, trust it
A longer document with more diagrams
A vote from the whole company

explanation: A design decision without visible alternatives is unreviewable — you can't evaluate a choice without knowing what it was chosen over and why.

prompt: A Code Review discussion turns into disagreement about naming conventions with no clear stakes either way. What's the pragmatic move?

options.text: Escalate to a company-wide policy meeting
Defer to the existing project convention and move on
Block the PR until everyone agrees
Rewrite the whole codebase to the reviewer's preferred style

explanation: Low-stakes stylistic disagreements are exactly what existing conventions are for — consistency with what's already there beats re-litigating preference.

prompt: While doing Code Review, you spot that a retry loop has no backoff and no max-attempts limit. What's the risk, and the fix?

options.text: It can hammer a struggling downstream service into a full outage — add exponential backoff and a cap
No risk, retries are always safe
It's fine as long as the network is fast
It will only ever slow down the current request

explanation: Unbounded, immediate retries are a classic way client code turns a downstream service's brief hiccup into a full outage (a retry storm) — backoff and a cap are the standard mitigation.

prompt: A Code Review change looks correct but silently swallows exceptions in a catch block with an empty body. Why does this matter even if nothing crashes?

options.text: It's a valid pattern for production code
It makes the code run faster
It hides real failures, making future debugging much harder and masking data corruption
It doesn't matter, silence means success

explanation: An empty catch block doesn't prevent failure — it just prevents anyone from finding out about it, which is worse: the system keeps running in a broken state.

prompt: A Code Review-related monitoring dashboard shows p50 latency is fine but p99 latency has tripled. What does this pattern usually indicate?

options.text: The dashboard is broken
The whole system is uniformly slower
p99 doesn't matter if p50 is fine
A subset of requests are hitting a slow path (e.g. cache misses, a specific query) — most traffic is unaffected

explanation: A rising p99 with a stable p50 is the signature of a tail-latency problem affecting a minority of requests, not a system-wide slowdown — investigate what's different about the slow subset.

prompt: Leadership wants to skip Code Review entirely for a release to hit a deadline. As the tech lead, what's the responsible response?

options.text: Quantify the specific risk this introduces and propose a scoped exception with monitoring, not a blanket skip
Agree silently and hope nothing breaks
Skip it without telling anyone
Refuse to ship at all

explanation: Refusing outright or silently complying are both worse than giving leadership the actual risk trade-off so they can make an informed, accountable call — that's what the role is for.

prompt: Two senior engineers disagree sharply on a Code Review approach and it's stalling the team. What's the most effective way to unblock this?

options.text: Avoid the topic indefinitely
Let the more senior person always win
Have a public vote among the whole engineering org
Timebox a spike to gather real data (benchmarks, prototypes) that the disagreement can be resolved against

explanation: Opinion-based stalemates are best resolved with data, not seniority or popularity — a small timeboxed spike turns a subjective argument into an objective comparison.

prompt: Using SQL, you find a report has 15% duplicate rows. What's the first thing to check?

options.text: Whether a join condition is producing a fan-out (one-to-many match)
Ignore it since 15% seems small
Manually delete random rows until it looks right
Assume the source system is wrong and stop

explanation: Duplicate rows after a join are most often caused by a join key that isn't actually unique on one side, producing a fan-out — check the join logic before touching the data.

prompt: A SQL chart shows a metric spiking every Monday at 9am sharply, then dropping. What should you consider first?

options.text: Users only work on Mondays
It's always a security incident
A scheduled job or batch process running at that time, not a real usage spike
The chart library has a bug

explanation: A perfectly regular, sharply-timed spike is the signature of an automated/scheduled process, not organic user behavior — check for a cron job or batch load first.

prompt: Someone asks you to use SQL to prove a new feature "caused" a metric increase, with no experiment or control group. What's the honest response?

options.text: Make up a causal claim to keep them happy
Refuse to help at all
Just show the correlated chart since it's what they asked for
Explain that correlation without a controlled comparison can't establish causation, and propose an A/B test or before/after with a control

explanation: Without a control group or experiment design, you can show correlation at best — an honest analyst says so and proposes how to actually test causation.

prompt: Your SQL query runs fine on 10k rows in staging but times out on 50M rows in production. What's the most likely first culprit?

options.text: The production database is simply slower hardware
50M rows is always too many for any query
The query syntax is invalid
A missing index on a column used in a WHERE/JOIN clause

explanation: A query that scales badly with row count, rather than failing outright, points at a missing index causing a full table scan rather than an indexed lookup — check execution plan/indexes first.

prompt: A SQL report excludes a whole customer segment silently because of a WHERE clause that filters NULLs implicitly. How would you catch this?

options.text: Re-run the same query again
Trust the report since it ran without an error
Compare total row counts before and after each filter step against the source table
Assume the segment simply doesn't exist

explanation: Silent data loss from implicit NULL handling doesn't throw an error — the only reliable catch is auditing row counts at each transformation step against the source.

prompt: Using SQL, you find a strong correlation between ice cream sales and drowning incidents. What's the correct interpretation?

options.text: Ice cream causes drowning
Drowning causes ice cream sales
Both are driven by a third variable (hot weather), not one causing the other
The data must be fake

explanation: This is the classic confounding-variable example: a third factor (temperature) drives both, and treating the correlation as causal would be a real analytical error.

prompt: A stakeholder wants a SQL-based dashboard updated in real time, but the underlying data only refreshes nightly. What's the right move?

options.text: Build a fake real-time-looking refresh animation anyway
Silently ship it and hope nobody asks
Refuse to build the dashboard at all
Explain the actual refresh cadence and label the dashboard accordingly, rather than implying false real-time-ness

explanation: Implying real-time freshness when the underlying data is a day old will eventually mislead a decision — the responsible move is transparent labeling of actual data recency.

prompt: A SQL analysis of A/B test results shows a 2% lift with a p-value of 0.09. Leadership wants to ship it as a clear win. What's the accurate framing?

options.text: Rerun the test until it's significant
The result is not statistically significant at the conventional 0.05 threshold — frame it as inconclusive, not a proven win
P-values don't matter if the number went up
0.09 is basically the same as 0.05, ship it as a win

explanation: A p-value above the conventional 0.05 threshold means the result could plausibly be noise — calling it a clear win overstates the evidence, and re-running until significance is a well-known statistical malpractice (p-hacking).

prompt: You're asked to use SQL to segment users, but 30% of records have missing demographic fields. What's the most defensible approach?

options.text: Drop all rows with any missing field silently
Fill missing fields with a guessed average and treat it as real
Explicitly report the missing-data rate and analyze whether it's missing at random before drawing segment conclusions
Ignore the missing data problem entirely

explanation: Missing data that isn't random (e.g. a signup step some users skip) can bias segment conclusions — the defensible move is to surface and investigate the missingness pattern, not silently drop or fabricate it.

prompt: A colleague asks you to explain a SQL result in a way a non-technical exec can act on. What should the summary lead with?

options.text: The business implication and recommended action, with supporting numbers after
Just the raw numbers with no context
Every technical detail of the methodology first
A list of caveats with no conclusion at all

explanation: A non-technical audience needs the 'so what' up front — leading with methodology or an unresolved list of caveats buries the actionable insight they actually need.

Nothing, just plan around 2 weeks exactly
Ask for a 1-week estimate instead
What assumptions that estimate depends on, and what could make it longer

prompt: In a Prioritization exercise, the loudest stakeholder in the room insists their pet feature is the top priority with no supporting data. How do you handle it?

options.text: Dismiss it outright without discussion
Add it to the roadmap without evaluating it
Automatically prioritize it since they're loud/senior
Ask what evidence or customer signal supports that priority, and weigh it against other requests using the same criteria

explanation: Volume or seniority isn't evidence — applying the same evaluation criteria to every request, including asking for supporting data, keeps prioritization defensible.

prompt: Your Prioritization process ranks every request by potential revenue impact only. What's the risk of that single-criterion approach?

options.text: It makes prioritization faster, which is the only goal
There is no risk, revenue is all that matters
It can systematically ignore retention risks, tech debt, and small-but-critical fixes that don't show up as new revenue
It guarantees the best long-term outcome

explanation: A single-metric prioritization model has blind spots by construction — things that matter (churn prevention, technical health) but don't show up as direct new revenue get systematically deprioritized.

prompt: During Prioritization, five customers ask for the same feature in one week. What should you check before assuming it's a top priority?

options.text: Immediately promise it will ship next sprint
Build it exactly as each of the five described it
Whether those five represent a broader pattern across the customer base or a small vocal segment
Ignore it since it's only five people

explanation: A handful of vocal requests can be a real signal or a loud minority — checking whether it generalizes across the broader base is what separates anecdote from actual prioritization evidence.

prompt: In Prioritization interviews, a user says "I would definitely use this" about a hypothetical feature. How should you weigh that statement?

options.text: Treat stated future intent with caution — look for evidence of actual past behavior instead
Build the feature immediately based on this one quote
Ignore everything users say in interviews

Investigate whether the team is closing more small, easier deals instead of pursuing larger, harder-fought ones — a possible trade-off, not a pure win
Conclude deal size never matters if win rate is up
Just celebrate the higher win rate

explanation: A rising win rate paired with a falling deal size can indicate the team is chasing easier, smaller wins rather than pursuing higher-value opportunities — a real trade-off worth investigating, not an unambiguous improvement.

prompt: A new rep asks why Discovery Calls matters if they already have a great product to sell. What's the accurate answer?

options.text: Even a great product needs a clear articulation of the prospect's specific problem to create urgency and justify the purchase
Skipping it saves time with no real downside
Only weak products need a sales process
It doesn't matter, a great product sells itself

explanation: Even genuinely great products rarely sell themselves without a clear connection to the specific buyer's problem and urgency — that connection is exactly what a disciplined sales process establishes.

prompt: During a Objection Handling, a prospect gives a vague answer like "we're looking to improve efficiency." What's the best follow-up?

options.text: Assume you already know what they mean
Ask for a specific example of where inefficiency is costing them time or money today
Move on to pitching your product's features
End the call since the answer wasn't detailed enough

explanation: Vague pain statements need to be grounded in a concrete example before you can qualify or pitch effectively — specifics reveal whether there's a real, sizable problem.

prompt: In Objection Handling, a prospect says "it's too expensive" right after seeing pricing. What does this usually signal?

options.text: The deal is definitely dead
They are lying about their budget
A value gap — they haven't yet connected the price to a clear enough return, not necessarily that the number itself is wrong
You should immediately offer a discount

explanation: Price objections immediately after seeing a number are often really about unclear value, not the number itself — the productive move is reconnecting price to the specific outcome, not jumping straight to a discount.

prompt: Your Objection Handling shows a large deal sitting in the same stage for two months with no activity logged. What should you do?

options.text: Mark it closed-lost automatically after any inactivity
Increase its forecasted probability since it's been open a long time
Re-engage the prospect directly to confirm real status rather than leaving it stale in the forecast
Leave it as-is since it's a big deal and might still close

explanation: A stale deal with no activity is a forecasting risk hiding in plain sight — confirming real status directly is better than assuming either continued momentum or automatic loss.

prompt: During Objection Handling, the champion you've been talking to suddenly goes quiet for three weeks. What's the most useful next move?

options.text: Wait indefinitely for them to respond
Send the exact same follow-up email daily
Assume the deal is dead and stop all outreach
Try reaching other stakeholders you identified earlier, since champions can lose influence, change roles, or get reassigned

explanation: Over-reliance on a single champion is a known deal risk — when they go dark, multi-threading to other stakeholders protects the deal instead of leaving it entirely dependent on one contact reappearing.

prompt: A prospect in Objection Handling objects "we already have a solution for this." What's the most useful response?

options.text: Ignore the objection and keep pitching the same points
Ask what's working and not working about the current solution to find a real gap or switching trigger
Immediately concede and end the conversation
Insist their current solution is bad without evidence

explanation: An existing solution objection is an opportunity to learn the real gap, if any exists — conceding immediately or arguing without evidence both skip the actual discovery that determines if there's a legitimate opportunity.

prompt: Your manager asks you to inflate a deal's forecast probability to hit team targets for the quarter. What's the professional response?

options.text: Inflate it but only slightly so it's less noticeable
Report a different number to your manager than what's in the actual system
Decline and explain that accurate forecasting protects the whole team's planning, even if the near-term number looks worse
Inflate it since the manager asked

explanation: Forecast integrity affects hiring, resourcing, and investor commitments downstream — inflating it to look better this quarter creates a bigger, compounding problem later, and the honest number is always the professional answer regardless of what's requested.

prompt: During Objection Handling, you realize the prospect's actual use case doesn't fit your product well at all. What's the right move?

options.text: Push forward anyway to hit your number
Quietly let the deal die without saying anything
Oversell features that don't really apply to their case
Tell them honestly, even if it costs you the deal, rather than force-fitting a bad match

explanation: Forcing a bad-fit deal through usually produces churn, refunds, and reputational damage that costs far more than the one deal — honest disqualification protects both the prospect and your long-term pipeline health.

prompt: A prospect asks for a feature your product doesn't have and says the deal depends on it. What's the disciplined response?

options.text: Refuse to discuss the request at all
Promise it will ship soon regardless of the actual roadmap
Say the feature already exists
Clarify the underlying need, check the real roadmap status, and set honest expectations rather than promising something uncertain

explanation: Promising uncertain roadmap items to close a deal creates downstream trust and churn problems — understanding the real underlying need and giving an honest roadmap answer is the disciplined path even under deal pressure.

prompt: A Campaign Analysis report shows a campaign has a high click-through rate but very low conversion. What's a likely explanation?

options.text: The tracking pixel is definitely broken
The ad promises something the landing page doesn't clearly deliver, causing a mismatch
Conversion rate never matters if CTR is good
High CTR always means the campaign is succeeding

explanation: A CTR/conversion mismatch is a classic sign of a promise-delivery gap between the ad and the landing experience — the ad is compelling enough to click, but something after the click isn't matching expectations.

prompt: Your Campaign Analysis plan is based entirely on one competitor's approach with no adaptation to your own audience. What's the risk?

options.text: Competitors always have worse strategies than you'd invent yourself
There's no risk, copying proven approaches always works
It guarantees the same results they got
Their audience, positioning, and resources may differ significantly, so copying tactics without adaptation can miss what actually works for your audience

explanation: Tactics that work for one brand's specific audience and positioning don't automatically transfer — copying without adapting to your own audience's actual context is a common and avoidable mistake.

prompt: A Campaign Analysis piece gets huge traffic but almost no engagement (comments, shares, time on page). What should you check?

options.text: Assume more traffic is always better regardless of engagement
Whether the traffic source matches your actual target audience, or if it's low-intent/low-relevance traffic
Assume the content itself must be terrible
Immediately delete the content

explanation: High traffic with low engagement often points at a traffic-quality or audience-mismatch problem rather than a content-quality problem — checking the traffic source is the useful next step.

prompt: Your Campaign Analysis strategy chases a trending topic unrelated to your actual product just for visibility. What's the downside?

options.text: It's risk-free as long as engagement numbers go up
There's no downside if it gets more views
It can attract attention from an audience that has no reason to become customers, wasting effort without building a relevant audience
It always improves brand perception

explanation: Chasing irrelevant trends can generate vanity metrics (views, brief attention) without building an audience that has any reason to convert — visibility isn't the same as relevant reach.

prompt: Your Campaign Analysis rankings for a key page dropped sharply after a site redesign. What's the most likely cause to investigate first?

options.text: Search engines randomly penalize redesigned sites
It must be a manual penalty from the search engine
Whether the redesign changed URLs, page structure, or content in ways that broke existing search signals
Rankings never relate to site structure

explanation: Ranking drops right after a redesign are most often self-inflicted — changed URLs, lost internal links, or altered content structure are the first things to audit before assuming an external cause.

prompt: Leadership wants your Campaign Analysis to claim credit for a revenue increase that coincided with a major product launch and a price change in the same month. What's the accurate framing?

options.text: Acknowledge multiple factors changed simultaneously and it's hard to isolate marketing's specific contribution without more careful analysis
Avoid discussing attribution at all
Claim marketing caused none of it
Claim marketing caused all of the increase

explanation: When multiple significant changes happen in the same period, attributing the full outcome to any single one overstates what you can actually know — an honest analysis acknowledges the confound rather than claiming full credit.

prompt: A Campaign Analysis campaign performs great in testing but underperforms at full scale. What's a common reason for this gap?

options.text: The original test must have been fraudulent
The test audience (often early adopters or a narrow segment) doesn't represent the broader audience reached at scale
Scaling a campaign always improves performance automatically
Full-scale campaigns always underperform regardless of quality

explanation: Small-scale tests often reach an unrepresentative early-adopter or narrow segment audience — performance regressing at broader scale is a well-known pattern, not necessarily a sign anything was done wrong.

prompt: Sales blames your Campaign Analysis for poor lead quality, while your dashboards show record lead volume. How do you resolve the disagreement productively?

options.text: Accept blame immediately without investigating
Insist your dashboards are the only truth that matters
Align on a shared definition of lead quality (e.g. close rate, fit criteria) rather than arguing volume vs. quality past each other
Stop generating leads until the disagreement resolves itself

explanation: Volume and quality are different metrics measuring different things — the productive path is agreeing on what 'quality' actually means together, not defending one metric against a complaint about a different one.

prompt: Your Campaign Analysis budget is being cut by 40% mid-quarter. What's the most disciplined response?

options.text: Cut every channel by exactly 40% evenly
Ignore the cut and overspend anyway
Reprioritize spend toward the channels/tactics with the best proven return, cutting the weakest performers first
Cut the newest initiatives regardless of performance

explanation: An across-the-board even cut ignores that channels have different returns — the disciplined response protects your best-performing spend and cuts the weakest first, using actual performance data to guide the reduction.

prompt: A junior marketer asks why Campaign Analysis needs a measurable goal if the content is "obviously good." What's the accurate answer?

options.text: Good content always performs well regardless of goals
If it's good, measurement is unnecessary
Subjective quality doesn't tell you whether the content achieved a specific business outcome — a measurable goal connects the work to real impact
Measurable goals only matter for paid ads

explanation: Perceived quality and measurable business impact are different things — a piece can be well-crafted and still fail to move the specific goal it was meant to support, which is exactly why a defined metric matters.

options.text: It's not worth investigating a small difference
The bank made an unexplainable error
A transposition or single missing/extra transaction entered as a round number
Currency conversion rates changed

explanation: A clean, round-number discrepancy is a classic signature of a data-entry error (transposed digits, a missed or duplicated entry) — checking recent entries near that amount is the efficient first step.

prompt: Your Financial Reconciliation shows actual spend tracking well under budget for a department three months running. What should you verify before praising efficiency?

options.text: Nothing, under-budget is always simply good news
Whether spend is under-tracked/miscoded rather than genuinely under budget, and whether planned initiatives are actually happening
Immediately cut their budget further
Assume the department is being deliberately wasteful elsewhere

explanation: Consistent, significant under-spend can reflect miscoded transactions or delayed/incomplete initiatives just as easily as genuine efficiency — verifying which it is prevents both false praise and a premature budget cut.

prompt: A manager asks you to move an expense into next quarter's Financial Reconciliation to make this quarter's numbers look better. What's the correct response?

options.text: Decline — expenses belong in the period they were actually incurred, and shifting them misstates financial reality
Do it but keep a private note about it
Do it only if the manager insists strongly
Do it since it's a small amount

explanation: Shifting expenses between periods to manage appearance is a form of misstatement regardless of size or how insistent the request is — the correct accounting period is when the expense was actually incurred.

prompt: Your Financial Reconciliation for the quarter shows a large unexplained variance in one account. What's the disciplined next step?

options.text: Adjust the number to match expectations without explanation
Wait until next quarter to see if it resolves itself
Note it as 'immaterial' without investigation since it's just one account
Trace the variance back to specific underlying transactions until the cause is identified, not just noted as an estimate

explanation: An unexplained variance should be traced to its root transactions, not smoothed over or waited out — 'immaterial' and 'unexplained' are not the same thing, and only investigation can tell you which applies.

prompt: Department heads consistently pad their Financial Reconciliation requests, anticipating cuts. What's a healthier system-level fix?

options.text: Publicly call out departments that pad requests
Cut every request by the same percentage automatically
Build trust through transparent, collaborative budget reviews so padding isn't the rational strategy anymore
Approve every request as submitted with no review

explanation: Padding is usually a rational response to an adversarial budget process — fixing the underlying incentive through transparency addresses the root cause better than blanket cuts or public shaming, which just reinforce the same dynamic.

prompt: Your Financial Reconciliation shows revenue up but cash flow down in the same period. What should you investigate?

options.text: Assume the two numbers must be measurement errors
Ignore it since revenue is the more important number
Whether receivables are growing (revenue booked but not yet collected) — a common driver of this specific divergence
Conclude revenue and cash flow are unrelated concepts

explanation: Rising revenue with falling cash flow is a well-known pattern usually driven by growing receivables (booked but uncollected revenue) — investigating collections is the natural next step, not dismissing either number.

prompt: Leadership asks you to classify a recurring operating cost as a one-time item in your Financial Reconciliation to improve a key metric's optics. What's the correct response?

options.text: Decline — misclassifying a recurring cost as one-time distorts the metric's meaning for anyone relying on it
Reclassify it but flag it only internally, not in the actual reporting
Do it only this one time as a favor
Do it since leadership requested it

explanation: Classification exists to make numbers meaningful and comparable — misclassifying a recurring cost as one-time to flatter a metric undermines the very purpose of the reporting, regardless of who requests it.

prompt: Your Financial Reconciliation process relies on a single person's manual spreadsheet with no backup or review. What's the risk, and the fix?

options.text: The risk only matters for very large companies
A single point of failure for critical financial data — introduce a second reviewer and a documented, backed-up process
Spreadsheets are inherently safer than any system
No real risk if that person is reliable

explanation: A single unreviewed spreadsheet controlling critical financial data is a classic single-point-of-failure and control weakness, regardless of how reliable the person is — a second reviewer and documented process is the standard mitigation.

prompt: An auditor flags a control weakness in your Financial Reconciliation process that management wants to dispute rather than fix. What's the responsible path?

options.text: Fix it only cosmetically without addressing the actual control gap
Ignore the finding since audits are often wrong
Dispute it regardless of merit to avoid the appearance of a problem
Evaluate the finding on its merits and, if valid, address the underlying control gap rather than just contesting the finding
